screens.title: Managing Variables and Facts
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how variables make Ansible playbooks adaptable and how facts let your automation respond to real system characteristics. Variables replace hardcoded values so the same playbook can run in development, staging, and production simply by changing inventory or extra variables. Facts are automatically gathered information about each host — operating system family, IP addresses, memory, and more — that your playbook can read to make decisions. Together, variables and facts let you keep playbooks generic but precise. For example, you might set a default web port in a playbook and override it for production with an extra variable on the command line, or use the ansible_os_family fact to install the correct package name for the host. We'll show how to define variables at different scopes, explain Ansible's precedence rules so you avoid surprising overrides, and demonstrate a short hands-on activity that creates users from host_vars and prints facts with debug. By the end you’ll understand where to place values, how to override them safely, and how to use facts to make conditional logic reliable.

screens.title: Why variables matter
screens.narratorSegment: Variables are the foundation of reusable Ansible automation. Instead of embedding specific values inside tasks or templates, you name a value and reference it throughout a playbook. This change makes the playbook portable: the same template or task can run against multiple environments where only the variable definitions differ. A concrete example: imagine an nginx configuration template that references a variable for the listening port. In staging you might set nginx_port to 8080 in group_vars, while production sets it to 80 in host_vars or via an extra-vars override. When the play runs, the template renders the correct port without changing the playbook. A common misconception is that variables are only about convenience; in practice they are essential for maintainability, testing, and reducing duplication. Another mistake is scattering the same variable name across multiple scopes without understanding precedence; we will address that explicitly later. Key takeaway: use variables to separate configuration data from orchestration logic, and keep variable names meaningful so they document intent. How could you name a variable so another engineer immediately understands its purpose? Why variables matter means variables store values that make playbooks adaptable and avoid hardcoding across environments.. In practical terms, replace hardcoded values with scoped placeholders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why variables matter

Replace hardcoded values with scoped placeholders so a single playbook works in many environments.
Concrete example
nginx_port: 8080
# Rendered in template as {{ nginx_port }}
Explanation
  • Variables separate data from tasks and templates, enabling reuse and reducing duplication.
  • They allow environment-specific values without changing playbook logic or templates.
  • Meaningful names document intent and make collaboration safer.
  • Avoid scattering identical names in many places without an intended precedence strategy.
Key Takeaway

Use variables to make playbooks generic and maintainable; give them descriptive names and control where they are defined.

Analogy & Common mistake
Think of variables as the knobs on a machine: tasks are the machine, variables tune behavior. A frequent error is assuming a lower-precedence variable will win; later we will show the precedence chain and an example with extra-vars overriding a playbook default.
Try this thought exercise
Name a variable for application log location that works across systems and explain where you'd place it by default.

screens.title: Variable scopes in Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible supports several variable scopes, and each scope determines where the value is defined and how long it applies. The common scopes we use are playbook vars, host_vars, group_vars, and extra-vars from the command line. Playbook variables are defined under the vars: keyword inside a play and apply only to that play. Host_vars are files named for each host in inventory/host_vars and give a specific host its own values. Group_vars define values for a collection of hosts — for example, a webservers group — and are perfect for environment or role-based defaults. Extra variables passed with -e or --extra-vars on the command line have a very high precedence, which makes them useful for one-off overrides or automation pipelines. A practical pattern is to set sensible defaults in group_vars, override environment-specific values in host_vars when necessary, and use extra-vars only for intentional overrides. The following step list clarifies when to choose each scope and offers a mnemonic: Default in group, specific in host, override on the command line. What scope would you use to change a port for a single host temporarily?

keyIdea.text: Choose group_vars for defaults, host_vars for per-host specifics, playbook vars for play-local defaults, and extra-vars for intentional overrides.

content.html:
Definition & Scope

Variable scopes in Ansible

Understand where to place values and the role each scope plays in deployment patterns.

Process: Choose a scope
  1. Start with group_vars for sensible environment or role defaults that apply to many hosts.
  2. Use host_vars for per-host exceptions or identifiers that must differ per machine.
  3. Use playbook vars for defaults tied to a specific play's intent and not reusable elsewhere.
  4. Use extra-vars for deliberate overrides at runtime, such as CI/CD pipelines or one-off runs.
Pro tip

Prefer group_vars for environment defaults and reserve extra-vars for explicit overrides to avoid accidental changes.

Examples
Playbook vars (vars:)
Set a default app_version for this play only.
host_vars/host1.example.com.yml
username: devops_user1
user_comment: "First DevOps User"
Extra-vars example
ansible-playbook play.yml -e "nginx_port=80 app_env=production"

screens.title: Playbook variables in use

In the play we name nginx_port and app_version under vars:, which makes those values available to every task in that play. A typical task uses the template module to render a configuration file that references {{ nginx_port }}. This pattern is common: keep the playbook logic generic and delegate environment-specific data to vars. Note that vars in a playbook are scoped to that play; they won't automatically affect other plays unless explicitly duplicated. A common misconception is to place sensitive data in plain vars: avoid hardcoding secrets. Instead, use Ansible Vault for secrets. In this example the play demonstrates the mechanism; later we'll show how inventory and extra-vars can override these values. Try changing nginx_port in the play and rerunning the template task to confirm the rendered file shows the new port. content.html:
Playbook Example

Playbook variables in use

A clear example showing vars: and how tasks reference those values.
Code walkthrough
---
- name: Configure web server
  hosts: webservers
  vars:
    nginx_port: 8080
    app_version: "1.2.3"
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Nginx is configured on port {{ nginx_port }}
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
This play defines nginx_port and app_version. Any task in the play can reference these variables using double curly braces. The template module renders files with those values at runtime.
Explanation & Example
- The vars: section is ideal for play-scoped defaults.
- To change the port for production without editing the playbook, pass an extra-var or set a host_var.
Common mistake: hardcoding values across multiple plays makes maintenance harder.
Key Takeaway

Use playbook vars for defaults tied to the play. For environment or host differences, prefer inventory scopes or extra-vars.

screens.title: Host and group variables
screens.narratorSegment: Inventory variables are loaded automatically based on the target hosts and groups. Host variables live in files named for each host inside host_vars/, for example host_vars/host1. example. com. yml. Use host_vars when a value is unique to a machine, such as a username or server_id. Group variables live in group_vars/groupname. yml and apply to every host in that group; those are ideal for role- or environment-wide defaults like nginx_port in a webservers group. This structure keeps environment configuration out of playbooks and in a dedicated inventory layout. A practical rule is: put defaults in group_vars, exceptions in host_vars. A common misconception is that inventory variables are always global; they only apply when the play targets the matching host or group. Another useful pattern is to maintain different inventories for staging and production, each with their group_vars adjusted accordingly. Organizing variables in inventory makes audit and review easier and prevents accidental changes to play logic. In practical terms, organize inventory with host_vars and group_vars for environment-specific configuration. content.html:
Inventory Variables

Host and group variables

Store environment and host-specific settings in host_vars and group_vars so playbooks remain generic.
Host variable example
# inventory/host_vars/host1.example.com.yml
nginx_port: 8080
server_id: "WEB01"
This file applies only when Ansible targets host1.example.com. Files in host_vars are loaded automatically at runtime.
Group variable example
# inventory/group_vars/webservers.yml
nginx_port: 80
default_app_version: "1.0.0"
Values here apply to every host in the webservers group. Group_vars is great for role- or environment-level defaults.
Best practices
  • Keep environment data in inventories, not in playbooks, for clearer separation of concerns.
  • Use separate inventory directories for staging and production if structure diverges.

screens.title: Extra variables (-e) and overrides
screens.narratorSegment: Extra variables passed with -e are a deliberate override mechanism. Because they sit high in Ansible's precedence order, an extra-var will almost always win against values defined in playbook vars, group_vars, or host_vars. This makes extra-vars useful for one-off runs, automation pipelines, or emergency changes that you do not want to commit into inventory. Use them cautiously: they can mask configuration issues if used ad hoc and make runs harder to reproduce if the override isn't tracked. A safe pattern is to use extra-vars in automation jobs where the override is documented in the deployment pipeline, and to prefer inventory changes for persistent differences. You can also pass a YAML file with -e @filename. yml for complex overrides. A common mistake is expecting a group_vars value to take precedence over a playbook var or extra-var; remember: extra-vars have very high priority. Practice by running a play with a default port defined in the play and then overriding it on the command line to observe the change. Extra variables (-e) and overrides means use -e for intentional overrides; remember they have higher precedence than most other variable sources.. In practical terms, use extra-vars to deliberately override values at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Override Mechanism

Extra variables (-e) and overrides

Command-line override
ansible-playbook configure_app.yml -e "app_port=80 app_env=production"
# or with a file
ansible-playbook configure_app.yml -e @prod_vars.yml
Extra-vars provide a direct way to change values for a run without editing inventory or playbooks.
When to use
  • CI/CD pipelines that inject environment-specific values.
  • Temporary overrides during debugging or emergency fixes.
  • Passing sensitive values from a secure pipeline step (prefer Vault for long-term secrets).
Common Mistake

Relying on ad-hoc extra-vars in local runs without recording them can cause irreproducible deployments. Use documented pipeline overrides for consistency.

screens.title: What are Ansible facts?
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible facts are variables automatically collected by the setup module at the start of most plays. Facts describe the host: operating system family, network interfaces, default IP addresses, memory, C P U, and other system details. These variables are prefixed with ansible_ and can be referenced in templates and conditionals, for example ansible_os_family or ansible_default_ipv4. address. To view facts for a host, run ansible host -m setup. Facts make playbooks intelligent: you can write conditional tasks that run only when a host matches a required property. For example, install httpd on Red Hat families and apache2 on Debian families using when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat" or "Debian". A common misconception is that facts are static; they reflect the state at the time they are gathered and can change between runs. If you disable gather_facts, your playbook will not have access to these variables unless you run the setup module explicitly. Facts are powerful for building cross-platform playbooks without branching out separate code for each system. What are Ansible facts? means facts are system properties collected by the setup module and available as ansible_ prefixed variables for logic and templates.. In practical terms, automatically gathered system information from managed hosts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition

What are Ansible facts?

Facts are gathered automatically to describe each managed host so playbooks can make informed decisions.
Show facts
ansible myhost -m setup

# Example fact usage in a task
- name: Print OS family
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "This host is part of the {{ ansible_os_family }} family."
Facts are available after gather_facts runs. If gather_facts is disabled, run the setup module explicitly to collect them.
Practical uses
  • Conditional tasks based on ansible_os_family.
  • Templates that pick addresses using ansible_default_ipv4.address.
  • Selecting packages, paths, or service names per host characteristics.
Key Takeaway

Facts let playbooks adapt to the actual properties of each host, making cross-platform automation practical.

screens.title: Using facts for conditional tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Facts become most useful when combined with conditionals. A common real-world requirement is to install the appropriate web server package depending on the operating system family. Ansible makes this straightforward: the ansible_os_family fact tells you whether the host is RedHat or Debian based, and you use a when: clause to control which package module runs. For example, use the dnf module with name: httpd when ansible_os_family == "RedHat", and apt with name: apache2 when ansible_os_family == "Debian". This approach keeps a single playbook that intelligently adapts its actions to each host. A common misconception is that facts are always identical across distributions; package names and service names still differ and must be handled explicitly. After running the play, verify with debug tasks that the correct branch executed by printing ansible_os_family and the package result. This strategy reduces duplicated playbooks and keeps maintenance centralized while ensuring each host receives the right package. Using facts for conditional tasks means use facts like ansible_os_family with when: to run distribution-specific tasks from a single playbook.. In practical terms, adapt tasks to the host's os family and properties. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Conditional example
keyIdea.text: Use facts like ansible_os_family with when: to run distribution-specific tasks from a single playbook.

content.html:
Conditional Logic

Using facts for conditional tasks

Task snippet
---
- name: Install web server package based on OS family
  hosts: all
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Install Apache on Red Hat-based systems
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: httpd
        state: latest
      when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat"

    - name: Install Apache on Debian-based systems
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: apache2
        state: latest
      when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"
Run this play to confirm the correct task runs per host. Use debug messages to print the evaluated ansible_os_family for each host as a verification step.
Explanation
  • when: checks facts at runtime and gates task execution.
  • Use distribution-specific package modules for best results (apt vs dnf).
  • Always verify by printing ansible_os_family and related facts after a run.
Check your understanding

How would you extend this pattern to handle a package name change in an OS derivative? Consider adding a mapping variable keyed by ansible_distribution.

screens.title: Precedence: which value wins?
screens.narratorSegment: When the same variable name appears in multiple places, Ansible resolves which value to use based on a precedence order. While the full precedence list is long, the simplified chain used most often runs from role defaults at the low end, through inventory variables, playbook vars, and role vars, to extra-vars at the top. Concretely: role defaults are the most permissive baseline, inventory group_vars and host_vars provide environment and host-specific defaults, play vars set play-scoped values, and extra-vars passed with -e override nearly everything. This matters because expecting a lower-precedence variable to override a higher-precedence definition is a common source of bugs. For example, putting a default in group_vars and then attempting to override it by changing a playbook var will not work if an extra-var was supplied; the extra-var would still win. A practical troubleshooting approach is to print the variable using debug in the play to see which value Ansible actually selected. Always document overrides and reserve extra-vars for deliberate changes so runs remain reproducible. Precedence: which value wins? means extra-vars typically override playbook, inventory, and role defaults; know the chain so you can predict final values.. In practical terms, understand the common chain of variable priority to avoid surprises. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Variable Precedence

Precedence: which value wins?

Simplified precedence (low → high)
Role defaults
Inventory variables (group_vars / host_vars)
Playbook vars (vars:)
Role vars
Extra variables (-e)
To resolve conflicts, determine where each value is defined and apply the precedence chain. If a value appears unexpectedly, add a debug task to print the variable and its origin, or use -vvv to inspect variable loading during a run.
Troubleshooting
- Use a debug task: ansible.builtin.debug: var=your_var to see the selected value.
- Check inventory and playbook for duplicate names and remove ambiguity.
- Reserve extra-vars for intentional, documented overrides.
Common Mistake

Expecting a lower-precedence value to override a higher-precedence one leads to confusing behavior. Always check the precedence chain when conflicts appear.

screens.title: Secrets, safety, and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Handling sensitive information requires care. Never hardcode passwords or A P I keys directly into playbooks or inventory files that might be checked into version control. The recommended approach is to use Ansible Vault to encrypt secrets and reference them as variables at runtime. This keeps the variable names in playbooks but stores the sensitive values encrypted. Another frequent error is defining the same sensitive variable in multiple places and accidentally exposing it with higher precedence; audit variable locations and avoid duplication. For non-sensitive configuration, keep defaults in group_vars and put host-specific identifiers in host_vars. In troubleshooting, remember that disabling gather_facts will remove access to ansible_ facts; only disable it when you know you won't need those variables. Finally, document any use of extra-vars in automation pipelines so overrides are transparent. The security discipline around variables prevents leaks and makes your automation safer for production environments. Secrets, safety, and common mistakes means encrypt sensitive variables with ansible vault and avoid duplicating secrets across multiple scopes to prevent accidental exposure.. In practical terms, avoid hardcoding sensitive data and learn safe patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Safety & Best Practices

Secrets, safety, and common mistakes

Protecting secrets
- Do not hardcode secrets into playbooks or inventory files that may be committed.
- Use Ansible Vault to encrypt passwords and API keys and reference the variables normally in runs.
- Store vault passwords securely in your CI/CD system when required for automated runs.
Other common mistakes
  • Expecting a group_var to override a playbook var without checking precedence.
  • Using extra-vars casually and creating irreproducible runs.
  • Disabling gather_facts when tasks depend on facts.
Pro tip

Track all overrides in automation pipelines and use Vault for persistent secrets to keep runs auditable and safe.

keyIdea.text: Practice placing variables in host_vars, creating users from those variables, and confirming facts with debug output.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Dynamic user creation and facts verification

Follow these templates and verify users and facts on each host.
Inventory file
[servers]
host1.example.com
host2.example.com
host_vars/host1.example.com.yml
username: devops_user1
user_comment: "First DevOps User"
host_vars/host2.example.com.yml
username: devops_user2
user_comment: "Second DevOps User"
Playbook template
---
- name: Create users and display facts
  hosts: servers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Create user {{ username }}
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: "{{ username }}"
        comment: "{{ user_comment }}"
        state: present
        shell: /bin/bash

    - name: Display host information
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Hostname: {{ ansible_hostname }}, OS Family: {{ ansible_os_family }}"
Run: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini dynamic_user.yml. Verify with id devops_user1 on host1 and inspect the debug output for each host to confirm facts.
Verification

Users created and debug messages show ansible_hostname and ansible_os_family for each host. Rerun with -e to test overrides.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how variables make Ansible playbooks adaptable and how facts let your automation respond to real system characteristics. Variables replace hardcoded values so the same playbook can run in development, staging, and production simply by changing inventory or extra variables. Facts are automatically gathered information about each host — operating system family, IP addresses, memory, and more — that your playbook can read to make decisions. Together, variables and facts let you keep playbooks generic but precise. For example, you might set a default web port in a playbook and override it for production with an extra variable on the command line, or use the ansible_os_family fact to install the correct package name for the host. We'll show how to define variables at different scopes, explain Ansible's precedence rules so you avoid surprising overrides, and demonstrate a short hands-on activity that creates users from host_vars and prints facts with debug. By the end you’ll understand where to place values, how to override them safely, and how to use facts to make conditional logic reliable.

These objectives focus your work with variables and facts so you can build robust, environment-aware automation. First, you will be able to explain why variables matter: they replace hardcoded values and let one playbook serve many environments. I will show a concrete example where a web port or application version differs between staging and production. Second, you'll learn how to define variables at multiple scopes — playbook vars, host_vars, group_vars, and extra-vars — and when to choose each. Third, you'll see Ansible facts: what they are, how the setup module collects them, and practical uses like choosing package names by operating system family. Finally, we'll cover variable precedence so you can predict which value wins when the same name appears in multiple places. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency by running a playbook and observing overridden values or printed facts.

This lab-focused objective explains the hands-on sequence you'll follow. First, you'll create an inventory with two hosts in a servers group and add separate host_vars files for each host to define username and user_comment. This practices inventory-scoped variables and shows how host-specific values propagate into tasks. Next, you will author a playbook that uses the ansible. builtin. user module to create accounts using the username and comment from host_vars, and then uses ansible. builtin. debug to print ansible_hostname and ansible_os_family to confirm facts are gathered. You will run the playbook normally and then again with --extra-vars to override a value, confirming the override behavior. Finally, the lab guides you to run ansible with the setup module to inspect all facts. The lab verifies you can place variables correctly, trigger an override with extra-vars, and use facts for conditional logic. This makes the abstract rules practical and testable.

Variables are the foundation of reusable Ansible automation. Instead of embedding specific values inside tasks or templates, you name a value and reference it throughout a playbook. This change makes the playbook portable: the same template or task can run against multiple environments where only the variable definitions differ. A concrete example: imagine an nginx configuration template that references a variable for the listening port. In staging you might set nginx_port to 8080 in group_vars, while production sets it to 80 in host_vars or via an extra-vars override. When the play runs, the template renders the correct port without changing the playbook. A common misconception is that variables are only about convenience; in practice they are essential for maintainability, testing, and reducing duplication. Another mistake is scattering the same variable name across multiple scopes without understanding precedence; we will address that explicitly later. Key takeaway: use variables to separate configuration data from orchestration logic, and keep variable names meaningful so they document intent. How could you name a variable so another engineer immediately understands its purpose? Why variables matter means variables store values that make playbooks adaptable and avoid hardcoding across environments.. In practical terms, replace hardcoded values with scoped placeholders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ansible supports several variable scopes, and each scope determines where the value is defined and how long it applies. The common scopes we use are playbook vars, host_vars, group_vars, and extra-vars from the command line. Playbook variables are defined under the vars: keyword inside a play and apply only to that play. Host_vars are files named for each host in inventory/host_vars and give a specific host its own values. Group_vars define values for a collection of hosts — for example, a webservers group — and are perfect for environment or role-based defaults. Extra variables passed with -e or --extra-vars on the command line have a very high precedence, which makes them useful for one-off overrides or automation pipelines. A practical pattern is to set sensible defaults in group_vars, override environment-specific values in host_vars when necessary, and use extra-vars only for intentional overrides. The following step list clarifies when to choose each scope and offers a mnemonic: Default in group, specific in host, override on the command line. What scope would you use to change a port for a single host temporarily?

Let's read a concrete playbook that defines local variables and uses them within tasks. In the play we name nginx_port and app_version under vars:, which makes those values available to every task in that play. A typical task uses the template module to render a configuration file that references {{ nginx_port }}. This pattern is common: keep the playbook logic generic and delegate environment-specific data to vars. Note that vars in a playbook are scoped to that play; they won't automatically affect other plays unless explicitly duplicated. A common misconception is to place sensitive data in plain vars: avoid hardcoding secrets. Instead, use Ansible Vault for secrets. In this example the play demonstrates the mechanism; later we'll show how inventory and extra-vars can override these values. Try changing nginx_port in the play and rerunning the template task to confirm the rendered file shows the new port. This confirms the variable is picked up at runtime and used by modules that consume templates or parameters. Playbook variables in use means define vars under the vars: keyword to provide play-local defaults consumed by tasks and templates.. In practical terms, walk through a play that defines vars and uses them in tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Inventory variables are loaded automatically based on the target hosts and groups. Host variables live in files named for each host inside host_vars/, for example host_vars/host1. example. com. yml. Use host_vars when a value is unique to a machine, such as a username or server_id. Group variables live in group_vars/groupname. yml and apply to every host in that group; those are ideal for role- or environment-wide defaults like nginx_port in a webservers group. This structure keeps environment configuration out of playbooks and in a dedicated inventory layout. A practical rule is: put defaults in group_vars, exceptions in host_vars. A common misconception is that inventory variables are always global; they only apply when the play targets the matching host or group. Another useful pattern is to maintain different inventories for staging and production, each with their group_vars adjusted accordingly. Organizing variables in inventory makes audit and review easier and prevents accidental changes to play logic. Host and group variables means use group_vars for shared defaults and host_vars for per-host specifics; inventory files are automatically loaded by ansible.. In practical terms, organize inventory with host_vars and group_vars for environment-specific configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Extra variables passed with -e are a deliberate override mechanism. Because they sit high in Ansible's precedence order, an extra-var will almost always win against values defined in playbook vars, group_vars, or host_vars. This makes extra-vars useful for one-off runs, automation pipelines, or emergency changes that you do not want to commit into inventory. Use them cautiously: they can mask configuration issues if used ad hoc and make runs harder to reproduce if the override isn't tracked. A safe pattern is to use extra-vars in automation jobs where the override is documented in the deployment pipeline, and to prefer inventory changes for persistent differences. You can also pass a YAML file with -e @filename. yml for complex overrides. A common mistake is expecting a group_vars value to take precedence over a playbook var or extra-var; remember: extra-vars have very high priority. Practice by running a play with a default port defined in the play and then overriding it on the command line to observe the change. Extra variables (-e) and overrides means use -e for intentional overrides; remember they have higher precedence than most other variable sources.. In practical terms, use extra-vars to deliberately override values at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ansible facts are variables automatically collected by the setup module at the start of most plays. Facts describe the host: operating system family, network interfaces, default IP addresses, memory, C P U, and other system details. These variables are prefixed with ansible_ and can be referenced in templates and conditionals, for example ansible_os_family or ansible_default_ipv4. address. To view facts for a host, run ansible host -m setup. Facts make playbooks intelligent: you can write conditional tasks that run only when a host matches a required property. For example, install httpd on Red Hat families and apache2 on Debian families using when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat" or "Debian". When the same variable name appears in multiple places, Ansible resolves which value to use based on a precedence order. While the full precedence list is long, the simplified chain used most often runs from role defaults at the low end, through inventory variables, playbook vars, and role vars, to extra-vars at the top. Concretely: role defaults are the most permissive baseline, inventory group_vars and host_vars provide environment and host-specific defaults, play vars set play-scoped values, and extra-vars passed with -e override nearly everything. This matters because expecting a lower-precedence variable to override a higher-precedence definition is a common source of bugs. For example, putting a default in group_vars and then attempting to override it by changing a playbook var will not work if an extra-var was supplied; the extra-var would still win. A practical troubleshooting approach is to print the variable using debug in the play to see which value Ansible actually selected. Always document overrides and reserve extra-vars for deliberate changes so runs remain reproducible. Handling sensitive information requires care. Never hardcode passwords or A P I keys directly into playbooks or inventory files that might be checked into version control. The recommended approach is to use Ansible Vault to encrypt secrets and reference them as variables at runtime. This keeps the variable names in playbooks but stores the sensitive values encrypted. Another frequent error is defining the same sensitive variable in multiple places and accidentally exposing it with higher precedence; audit variable locations and avoid duplication. For non-sensitive configuration, keep defaults in group_vars and put host-specific identifiers in host_vars. In troubleshooting, remember that disabling gather_facts will remove access to ansible_ facts; only disable it when you know you won't need those variables. Finally, document any use of extra-vars in automation pipelines so overrides are transparent. These are three core ideas to keep top of mind. First, a variable is a named placeholder used in playbooks and templates to avoid hardcoding configuration. Second, playbook variables, host_vars, and group_vars each provide a scope for where values live; choose the scope that matches the lifespan and breadth of the value. Third, extra-vars (-e) are high-precedence overrides used for deliberate changes at runtime. Remember these ideas as you write automation: name variables clearly, place them where they logically belong, and use extra-vars intentionally so runs remain reproducible.
